description:
Hi, I’m Nabin Joshi—a Robotics & AI Engineer and World Robot Olympiad (WRO) National Champion. I love turning raw space and Earth data into real, interactive tech using AI/Computer Vision (Python, TensorFlow), App/Backend Dev (Flutter, Flask, AWS), and 3D Visualization (Unreal Engine, Blender).

Why join? I focus on shipping a working, live prototype rather than just a slide deck, and our core AI, backend, and 3D pillars are already covered.
summary: VitalOrbit is a website that helps astronauts assess their own health when help from Earth is slow or far away. The astronaut logs eight quick measurements: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Each reading is colored green, amber or red, and the tool gives plain-language steps for what to do next. A clickable human body shows which organ is affected and which NASA spaceflight hazard (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile or closed environments) puts it at risk. Trend charts show slow drifts, and a red result prompts the crew to contact the flight surgeon. Daily missions, XP, streaks and badges keep astronauts checking in. The tool works offline and adapts its guidance for a space station, a deep-space spacecraft, the Moon or Mars. As missions get longer and more autonomous, early self-assessment helps prevent small problems from becoming critical.
details:
What it does: VitalOrbit is a Node.js and Express web app with five pages: Dashboard, Check-in, Trends, Missions and Guide. Astronauts enter their readings, each with a “how to measure and why it matters” explanation. The app compares each value to a reference range and shows it as In range, Watch or Act now. Every colored status is also written as a word, so color is never the only signal. The dashboard computes a health score and shows a clickable body. Each body part links its readings to the NASA hazard that affects it, with a source link. Advice is shown per reading, and a red reading raises a “Contact the flight surgeon” alert. Trend charts draw the readings over 7 to 90 days against colored safe zones, with a rising, falling or steady message. Data can be exported as CSV or sent to a simulated ground-team endpoint.

Benefits and impact: Astronauts on long missions must be able to catch health problems early without waiting for the ground. The tool is simple enough for non-experts, works offline because data stays on the device, and gives the flight surgeon a clear trend history.

Creativity: The body map ties each organ to its NASA hazard. Location modes change the guidance for a space station, spacecraft, Moon base or Mars base. Daily missions turn health habits into a streak and XP game.

Tools: Node.js, Express, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, canvas charts, browser localStorage. No database and no external libraries beyond Express.

Factors we considered: Reference ranges are simplified general adult clinical ranges, not NASA limits, because NASA’s public hazard pages don’t publish astronaut vital-sign limits. This is stated in the app. The tool is a prompt to look closer, not a diagnosis. Demo data is synthetic.
